title: In the 1730s a Ghana-born philosopher taught at German universities
body: Anton Wilhelm Amo was born around 1703 in Axim, in present-day Ghana, and taken to Amsterdam by the Dutch West India Company at about the age of four. Presented to the dukes of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel in 1707, he was raised in the ducal household, entered the law school at Halle in 1727, and in 1729 defended a thesis on **the rights of Africans in Europe**. A doctorate in philosophy followed at Wittenberg in 1734, and he went on to lecture at Halle and Jena. A hostile campaign and a public lampoon drove him back to Africa around 1747, where he died around 1759.

slides.heading: Mind and body
slides.text: His 1734 dissertation, On the Apathy of the Human Mind, argued for a broadly Cartesian dualism: mind and body are distinct kinds of thing. Four years later he published a treatise on the art of philosophising soberly and accurately.

slides.heading: Why he left
slides.text: Enemies in Halle staged a public lampoon of him. Amo sailed on a Dutch West India Company ship, arriving in Ghana about 1747, and was later taken to a fort at Shama, possibly to keep him from stirring dissent. The exact date and place of his death are unknown.

slides.question: When did Berlin finally rename its Mohrenstraße after Amo?
slides.explanation: Berlin-Mitte proposed the change in 2020, but objections kept it in court until 23 August 2025, when Mohrenstraße became Anton-Wilhelm-Amo-Straße. The street had carried its old name since 1707.

slides.label: the year Berlin renamed its Mohrenstraße after Amo, ending a long legal battle
slides.text: Stuttgart dedicated an Anton Wilhelm Amo Square in 2022, and two German exhibitions in 2024 were devoted to him.

slides.question: What was the subject of Amo’s 1729 thesis?
options: The rights of Africans in Europe
The geography of the Gold Coast
slides.explanation: De iure Maurorum in Europa, ‘On the rights of Moors in Europe’. The manuscript is lost, but a summary was published in 1730.
